Spring cavefish (Forbesichthys agassizii) inhabits subterranean streams and springs throughout the Cumberland Plateau, where stable thermal conditions prevail year-round. Field studies conducted at a consistent water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] have documented that the period from ovum activation to the emergence of the yolk-sac larva lasts approximately 30.5 days [ab = approximately 30.5 days], a developmental timeline that reflects the reduced metabolic rates characteristic of stygobitic fishes. Newly hatched prolarvae are lecithotrophic and measure about 0.0028 grams [Wwb = about 0.0028 grams] in wet weight, a value derived from the average egg diameter of 1.75 millimeters observed in gravid females. This modest neonatal mass, combined with a relatively extended incubation period, is consistent with the pattern seen in other amblyopsid cavefishes, where slow embryonic development is linked to the sparse organic carbon availability in aphotic environments.

Sexual maturation in Forbesichthys agassizii proceeds gradually under the cool, unvarying temperatures of its groundwater habitat. At 13 °C [T = 13 °C], individuals typically attain puberty approximately 8 months after hatching [tp = approximately 8 months after hatching], a duration that aligns with the 11-to-12-month interval to first reproduction reported in related troglobitic species. The standard length at which gonadal recrudescence becomes evident is 3.9 centimeters [Lp = 3.9 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight of roughly 0.52 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.52 grams]. This pubertal body mass, estimated from the allometric relationship between length and weight, represents a substantial fraction of the ultimate adult size and suggests that a critical threshold of somatic growth must be achieved before reproductive activation can occur.

As adults, Spring cavefish reach a maximum standard length of 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], corresponding to a total length of approximately 9 centimeters based on the observed morphometric ratio. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown individuals is estimated at 3.7 grams [Wwi = 3.7 grams], a figure that underscores the diminutive body plan typical of cave-adapted amblyopsids. This asymptotic mass, derived from length-weight regressions applied to field-captured specimens, indicates that energetic constraints in the oligotrophic spring environment limit overall body size. Comparisons with epigean cypriniform fishes of similar latitudes reveal that F. agassizii achieves only a fraction of the adult mass observed in surface-dwelling relatives, likely a consequence of reduced prey availability and low metabolic demand in the hypogean realm.

Reproductive output in this species is modest, consistent with its low-energy lifestyle. Under constant thermal conditions of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], females produce an average of 1.5 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 1.5 eggs per spawning event], with approximately 1.1 spawning events occurring each year [F_R_i = approximately 1.1 spawning events occurring each year]. This low fecundity, combined with the extended interval between spawning bouts, results in an annual reproductive rate that is among the lowest documented for North American cavefishes. The protracted reproductive schedule likely reflects the constraints imposed by sporadic food resources in the subterranean environment, where successful foraging events are unpredictable and energy reserves must be carefully managed to sustain both somatic maintenance and gamete production over the long term.

Longevity data for Forbesichthys agassizii remain limited, but studies on the closely related Amblyopsis rosae provide a useful benchmark. At 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum lifespan is estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years], a duration that is exceptionally long for a fish of such small body size and that aligns with the general life-history syndrome of cave-dwelling organisms, which typically exhibit delayed maturity, low fecundity, and extended lifespans. This extreme longevity, coupled with the slow pace of growth and reproduction observed in F. agassizii, suggests that the species has evolved a bet-hedging strategy adapted to the unpredictable and resource-limited conditions of its spring-fed habitat, where the probability of reproductive success in any given year is low but the cumulative opportunity over a decade-long reproductive window is maximized.
